title: Sunil Jain vs Manmeet Singh Pruthi on 23 February, 2026
full_text: Sunil Jain vs Manmeet Singh Pruthi on 23 February, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Sunil Jain Vs. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Acquitted 7. Date of judgment/order 23.02.2026. Date of Institution : 11.08.2016 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 15.01.2026 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 23.02.2026 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Manoj Tiwari. Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh. G.S Narula. CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 2 of 13 AASTHA SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:25 +0530 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Sh. Sunil Jain (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against Sh. Manmeet Singh Pruthi (hereinafter "accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant and the accused had friendly relations with each other and the complainant gave loan to accused from time to time, which the accused repaid in part and then stopped paying. That, after persistence of the complainant, the accused had issued several post-dated cheques to the complainant and his wife in discharge of his liability, details of which are as follows: (i) cheque bearing no. 072659 dated 23.04.2016 in the sum of Rs. 3,50,000/-, drawn on Corporation Bank,E-52-53, Mata Chowk, Mahipalpur, New Delhi. (ii) cheque bearing no. 409878 dated 07.05.2016 in the sum of Rs. 1,25,000/-, drawn on Canara Bank, East Patel Nagar, New Delhi-110008. B. That, on presentation of the aforesaid cheques in question by the complainant with his banker Axis Bank Ltd.,CR Park, New Delhi, the cheque no. 072659 was dishonoured with the remarks "funds insufficient" vide return memo dated 14.06.2016 and cheque no. 409878 was dishonoured with the remarks "Kindly Contact Drawer/Drawee Bank and Please Present Again" vide return memo dated 15.06.2016. AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 3 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:29 +0530 C. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 27.07.2016, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/Z and placed on record Cheques in question Ex. CW-1/A-1 to Ex. CW-1/A-2; Bank Return memos Ex. CW-1/B-1 to Ex. CW-1/B-2; Copy of legal demand notice and postal receipt Ex. CW-1/C & Ex. CW-1/D (Colly.) and Tracking Report Ex. CW-1/E (Colly). 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 08.11.2017 to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has accepted issuance of cheque in favour of the complainant and also his signatures on the cheque in question. The accused has denied receiving the legal demand notice. The accused has stated that he had issued undated cheques to the complainant 8-9 years as security to the complainant as the accused used to invest on behalf of the complainant and the accused had returned the entire invested amount but never asked for return of security cheques AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 4 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:33 +0530 from the complainant in good faith. The accused has stated that he does not owe the liability as stated by the complainant in the cheque in question. 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 23.01.2023. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 15.05.2023 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. DW-1 was examined, cross-examined and discharged. Vide order of this court, DE was closed by recording a separate statement of the accused. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 5 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:38 +0530 IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 6 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:44 +0530 from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheques, i.e., bearing no. 072659 dated 23.04.2026 for Rs. 3,50,000/- drawn on Corporation Bank,E-52-53, Mata Chowk, Mahipalpur, New Delhi and bearing no. 409878 dated 07.05.2016 for Rs. 1,25,000/- drawn on Canara Bank, East Patel Nagar, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/A1 to Ex. CW1/A2). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheques in dispute belong to him. It is also not disputed that the cheques in question are not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheques. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 7 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:49 +0530 vide return memos dated 14.06.2016 and 15.06.2016 (Ex. CW1/B1 to Ex. CW1/B2). By implication thereof, the cheques were presented within three months and the same were returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 27.06.2016 (Ex. CW1/C) was dispatched on 01.07.2016 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/D) (Colly.), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has not accepted the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC, however the address on legal demand notice is the address on statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and DE. Furthermore, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 8 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:54 +0530 in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 9 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:10:58 +0530 Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/Z and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. The case of the complainant is that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of his liability qua the loan taken from the complainant, as indicated by the complainant by his statement of account Ex. CW1/D1 (Colly.). The accused has taken a consistent defence and has stated that he had repaid the liability owed by him to the complainant. The accused has also placed on record proof of payment by bank transfer through his passbook Ex. DW1/A which indicates payment of installment in the sum of Rs. 5,85,371/- by way of account transfer via cheques and payment of Rs. 16,31,629/- by way of cash to the complainant between February 2009 to August 2013. The complainant has also admitted to some transactions of payment made by accused in his bank account, in his cross-examination dated 28.11.2022 by stating as follows: "Yes, the statement of the accused had returned some amount by cheque. The same is reflected in bank statement which is Ex. CW1/D1 (Colly.) which is already on record. The amount given by the accused which is reflected in bank statement on 23.03.2009, 03.02.2010, 16.08.2010, 25.03.2011, 27.03.2012, 08.11.2012, 04.06.2013 and 17.07.2013." AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 10 of 13 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:11:03 +0530 The complainant has further stated as follows: "...I gave first loan approximately Rs. 80,000/- to the accused around year 2005. At that time, as per my knowledge accused was in the business of crusher. I do not remember whether accused returned the aforementioned loan or not. I do not remember whether that aforementioned loan was given to accused in the form of cash or cheque..." On the one hand, the complainant is stating that he does not remember if the amount of Rs. 8,00,000/- was repaid by the accused or not. On the other hand, the complainant is claiming the amount from the accused in his ledger and indicating that as a liability without proving if the accused owes the same to him or not. Further, apart from the above transactions as stated by the complainant, the accused has placed on record his bank account statement Ex. DW1/A to indicate the payments made by him to the complainant to rebut the presumption that he does not owe the liability as mentioned by the complainant in her cheque in question. By placing his statement of account on record and the complainant also admitting to the repayment by the accused, the accused has rebutted the presumption to the extent of "preponderance of probabilities" and the onus of proof has shifted upon the complainant to prove that the accused owed the liability as stated by the complainant in her cheque in question. 19. In the present case, the complainant has failed to place anything on record to indicate the liability of the accused on the date of the presentation of the cheque in question. The accused, however, has placed on record proof of payment to rebut the presumption that the accused owes the liability as mentioned on the cheque in question. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Dashrathbhai Trikambhai Patel v. Hitesh M. Patel (2023) 1 SCC 578 has held that "for the commission of offence u/s 138 NI Act, the AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 11 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:11:08 +0530 cheque that is dishonoured must represent a legally enforceable debt on the date of maturity or presentation." The complainant failed to discharge the onus and no evidence was produced to show the actual liability of the accused on the date of presentation of the cheque in question. Moreover the complainant has not even mentioned about the repayment by the accused in the legal demand notice as well as in the evidence by way of affidavit. 20. The accused therefore has rebutted the presumption u/s 139 NI Act by proving that the liability of the accused is lesser than what has been stated by the complainant in the cheque in question, as certain payment has been made by the accused towards the liability. While, the complainant has been unsuccessful in proving that the accused owed the liability as stated in the cheque in question, despite the payment made by the accused as depicted by Ex. DW1/A, by placing on record any ledger or statement of account to indicate the liability of the accused on the date of presentation of the cheque in question. 21. In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this court has arrived at an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in its favour and by several inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. Once the accused had created a probable defence as to the legally enforceable liability, the onus shifted on the complainant to prove the existence of legally enforceable liability of the accused, as on the date of the drawal or presentation of the impugned cheques, which has not been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. Since this basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract liability under Section 138 NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly, no offence of dishonour of the impugned cheque under the said Section is made out. AASTHA CC No. 635298/2016 Sunil Jain Vs. Manmeet Singh Pruthi Page 12 of 13 SHARMA Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.02.23 16:11:13 +0530 22. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused Manmeet Singh Pruthi has been successful in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by punching holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence and as a consequence, questioning the existence of legally enforceable liability in favour of the complainant and that the cheque was not issued by the accused in discharge of existing legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant. In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Manmeet Singh Pruthi is hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. PRONOUNCED IN THE OPEN COURT TODAY ON 23rd February, 2026. This judgment consists of 13 pages and all pages are duly signed by me.
